newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzania finance minister implicated in graft probe.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania finance minister implicated in graft probe.

text.p: Tanzania's finance minister Simon Mbilinyi acted improperly over the importation of cooking oil and should be "taken to task", according to a government corruption probe report.
The report released on Tuesday said Mbilinyi ignored advice from his ministry officials who said the oil should not receive tax exemption.
There was no immediate comment from the minister on the report but he has consistently denied graft allegations in the past.
"The committee has advised that the president (Benjamin Mkapa) should take to task the minister in the way he will deem fit," according to the 42-page report by a National Assembly select committee.

"We do not have tangible evidence to substantiate corruption allegations against the minister. Circumstantial evidence suggests however that there was a motive that drove the minister to act against advice," said House Speaker Pius Msekwa, who released the findings at parliamentary offices in the capital.
The cooking oil exemption scandal has cast a shadow over Mkapa's efforts to crack down on corruption, seen as a key challenge facing his government.
The chairman of the main opposition party, Augustine Mrema, earlier accused senior ministers of accepting 900 million shillings ($1.5 million) in bribes to facilitate the tax waiver.

The exemptions were given to four local companies and covered a shipment of 4,700 tonnes of cooking oil. Importers were allowed to pay import duty at a concessional rate well below the amount stipulated in the June 20 budget.

A similar import tax exemption scandal discovered by the World Bank in 1994 led to the downfall of then finance minister Kighoma Malima and a suspension of $200 million in donor balance of payments support.
The committee also found that Mbilinyi acted improperly in sanctioning the reduction in the price of export fish fillets from Lake Victoria, a decision that gave traders a more favourable tax rate.
Msekwa's report recommended disciplinary action be taken against a number of government officials implicated in the alleged tax scam.
"Evidence has shown that normal procedures were flouted and expert advice from the ministry was ignored," the report said.
